$comment: Tunable constants for the whole game. Every number here is a dial, not a law. The web prototype reads these directly, so changing a value here changes the digital game AND the printed reference sheet.

currency.name: Coin
currency.$massNote:
A gold coin weighs 25 grams, and it is the one thing on this list that used to weigh nothing. Coin was on carrying.notCarried - an abstraction that lived outside the world - and a purse of four hundred is ten kilograms, which is most of what a figure can shoulder. So it comes off that list and goes on the scales with everything else: what you are carrying is what you are carrying, and a fortune is heavy.

It is a real weight for a real coin. A sovereign is eight grams and a piece of eight is twenty-seven; twenty-five puts this one in the same purse as the coins it is drawn from, and forty of them to the kilogram is arithmetic a table can do without being asked to.
currency.$carryNote: Forty coin to the kilogram. A strength-3 figure can shoulder 9 kg, so an empty-handed one could carry 360 coin and nothing else; the 60 they start with is a kilogram and a half, which is a rounding error against a sword. The weight only bites when somebody is moving a fortune - which is exactly the moment it should.

phases.name: Events
phases.summary: In turn order, each player reveals one event card and resolves it. A card's scope decides who it hits: global cards hit everyone, whoever drew them.

phases.name: Labour Roll
phases.summary: Each player rolls their effort dice: one die per worker. Pips = hours of effort available this round.

phases.name: Actions
phases.summary: In turn order, players spend effort, coin and commodities: allocate, build, move, trade, forage, fight.

phases.name: Production Tick
phases.summary: Advance every progress track: construction, crop growth, transport in transit, maturing goods.

phases.name: Feeding
phases.summary: Each town must pay food upkeep from stock held in or near that town. Shortfalls cause unrest. Then every player rolls the ochre spoil die once for each perishable stack they are still holding.

phases.name: Market
phases.summary: Roll the market for every line on the ledger: two blue, two red, one green, plus whatever the good's own nature adds. Read the swing ruler, walk the band, write the new price and strike the old one through. Turn order passes to the left.

effort.notes: Modifiers may (a) add flat hours, (b) step a worker's die up or down the ladder, or (c) grant extra dice. Resolve in that order: extra dice, then ladder steps, then flat bonuses.

foodVarietyBonus.effect: +1 flat effort to every worker in that town next round
foodVarietyBonus.summary: Feed a town from 3+ distinct food commodities in one Feeding phase to earn the variety bonus.

starvation.riotEffect: Workers in that town roll d4 instead of their normal die until unrest clears; one worker leaves the town at 5 unrest.
starvation.clearUnrest: Feeding a town fully in a later round removes 1 unrest; a feast (2 food per worker) removes 2.

population.notes: Specialists eat like everyone else, but a town without a fed specialist cannot run recipes that require that profession.

construction.notes: Materials are paid when the site is founded. Build points accumulate on a progress track; a building only produces once its track is full.

wear.$comment:
What using a thing does to it, and it is now one rule for every made thing in the game rather than a private arrangement between tools and their own file.

Tools wore out and nothing else did. A sword was immortal, a suit of plate never dented, a rope never frayed and a lantern burned forever - so the only equipment decision anybody ever made twice was which axe to buy. Everything a player carries wears now, on one track, in one unit, at one wear point a use.

THE SCALE IS THE BOARD'S. Wear used to run to thirty-four and be counted on the tool, because there was no track for it and the strip note said there never would be: 'it runs past twenty, the board stops at fourteen.' The board has a track for it now - four of them, one beside each kit slot - so the number came down to meet the board rather than the board going up to meet the number. That is the same trade the kilogram made when a hero could not stand their own load on a fourteen-rung ladder, and it is the right way round: the ceiling is the game's, and a number that will not fit under it is a number that is wrong.

Rescaling did not shorten anything's life, because the CLOCK changed with the scale. An axe had twenty-four wear at one a labour hour, which is eight three-hour jobs. It has ten at one a JOB, which is ten. A tool lasts slightly longer than it did and nobody adds hours up any more.
wear.track: The W track beside the item's own slot on the player board. Set it from the W box on the card when the thing is picked up, knock it down a rung each time the thing is used, and at 0 it is finished.
wear.printedOn: The card, as the W box in the summary strip: the most wear the thing will take. Nothing on a card ever moves - see data/playerboard.json.

takes.when: each recipe it is used in
takes.$note: Per job, not per hour. A worker who spends nine hours felling timber has run one job and blunted one axe by one.

takes.applies: a weapon, a shield, a helm or a suit of armour
takes.when: each round of a battle it is swung or worn in
takes.$note: Both sides, win or lose. A blow you turned still dented the plate.

takes.when: each night leg it is burned on
takes.$note: Which is what a torch is: one wear, one night, gone.

takes.when: each time its own card says
takes.$note: A rope that takes a party down a cliff, a grappling hook that holds, a bag that is stuffed past its seams. The card says what counts as a use, because a rope and a pair of boots do not wear for the same reason.

wear.atZero: Worn out. The card is discarded, the track is cleared, and whatever the thing was doing for its owner it stops doing at once - a broken tool does not refund the effort already spent on the job that broke it, and a sword that goes at 0 leaves you swinging with nothing for the rest of the battle.
neverWears: Potions, which are drunk rather than worn out - the card is discarded on use and there is no W box on it.
Talismans. Mana is not friction; a phylactery that has been filled and emptied a hundred times is a phylactery.
Commodities, which are counted rather than owned.

repair.$note: Any settlement with a blacksmith, three points a round, four coin a point and two hours of somebody's labour. A thing may be mended any number of times; what cannot be mended is a thing at 0, which is not damaged, it is gone.

wear.$boardNote: Four kit slots, four W tracks, so a player tracks the wear of everything they are actually carrying and nothing else. A fifth thing in play is a fifth thing whose wear nobody is counting, which is the same argument the four slots were already making.

tools.wearRule: rules.json wear - a tool is not special any more, it is the first thing that wore out.
tools.brokenToolEffect: Tool is removed from play. Effort already spent this round is not refunded.
tools.$sizesNote: A size used to multiply durability as well, and it does not any more. A bigger loom is a FASTER loom, not a longer-lived one - and a multiplied wear number is a number the ceiling sweep cannot see, because it never appears in the data at the size it is actually walked at. One multiplier fewer, one hole in the ceiling fewer, and one thing less to work out at a table.
tools.notes: Output multipliers round down, minimum 1. A size-3 tool never lets one worker exceed a site's worker cap - it just makes that worker's hours count for more.

storage.overflowRule: Commodities above capacity spoil at the end of the Feeding phase: lose half, rounded up.
storage.notes: Bulk values on commodities are slot costs. One slot holds one bulk point.

market.pricedBy: data/pricing.json. Every Market phase each town rolls two BLUE dice for demand, two RED for supply and one GREEN for volatility, per commodity line on the ledger, and reads the result on the swing ruler printed on the market board. The whole sum is addition: Demand − Supply + Volatility + whatever the good's own nature adds. Nothing multiplies and nothing is halved.
market.recordedOn: data/ledger.json - the price ledger. One column per commodity traded, one row per round, and the price written in three hollow seven-segment figures the player colours in, struck through when it changes and the new one written under it. No board tracks a price any more, and no token walks a band.
market.$bandNote: THE BANDS ARE A PRINTED ROW, NOT A LADDER. Every commodity's six prices are worked out from its base value and printed as one row of six figures in the annex - grain is 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 · 10 - so a price move is a step ALONG THAT ROW. The price you last wrote in the ledger is one of the six; the swing ruler says how many places to step; the figure you land on is the new price. There is nothing to multiply, no band index to remember and no bar to walk, which is what let the price ladder come off the market board without anything replacing it.

merchantStock.$comment: When a player meets a merchant - on the road via a discovery roll, or by visiting a settlement - shuffle the item deck and deal this many cards face up. That is what is for sale this visit, at base value +10%. Bigger places carry deeper stock.
merchantStock.notes: Tools may be bought the same way at any settlement with a blacksmith rank town or better: deal from the tool list instead.

market.notes: Base values live on each commodity. Town price = baseValue at the band its bar stands on, and every commodity's six prices are printed out in full in the annex so that lookup is never a multiplication. The spread is the house cut when trading with the board rather than another player. What moves a band is not here: it is data/pricing.json, because a die roll and four kinds of goods are a system rather than a constant.

infrastructure.$comment:
What a player gets for laying road and rail, beyond the fact that their own carts go faster on it. Roads were the one thing in the game you built for everybody and were paid for by nobody: the network victory condition scored them at the very end and nothing scored them in the twenty rounds before that, so a road only ever got built where its builder happened to want to walk.

Three returns, in the order a player feels them: a toll every time somebody else uses it, a better price for cargo that moves on your own network, and the network points that were already there. The toll is small on purpose - it is a reason to build, not a business - and it is collected from the table rather than paid into a bank, so every coin of it comes out of a rival.
infrastructure.ownership: A road, rail line or bridge belongs to the player who paid for it, for the rest of the game. Mark it with that player's route tokens (components.json tokens.route) as it is laid - the token IS the record, and an unmarked road belongs to nobody.

toll.collectedBy: The owner, from the moving player, the moment that leg ends.
toll.capNote: No leg pays more than this however long it is, so a trunk road across the continent is worth building and is never a tax gate.
waived: The owner's own figures, parties and cargo - you do not pay yourself.
Any party carrying a quest the owner accepted.
Any hex whose road the moving player also owns a share of, where two networks meet.
toll.refused: A player may decline to pay and go round. They may not decline to pay and go through.

haulage.rule: Cargo that starts or ends its journey in a settlement your own road or rail reaches sells for a tenth more than the town price.
haulage.why: A road is worth more to the person who built it than the toll on it will ever be. This is where the real money is, and it is why the sensible first road runs from your mine to your market rather than towards anybody else.

payback.$comment: The check that says the numbers are not decoration. A road hex costs 1 stone and 3 build points; stone is 5 coin, so call it 5 coin a hex and an hour a hex on top. At 1 coin a hex a stretch pays for itself after five foreign crossings, which in a four-player game is a handful of rounds on any road worth building. Rail costs 2 steel and 2 lumber - 70 coin a hex - and will never repay that in tolls alone: rail is repaid by the train that runs on it and by victoryPointsPerTile, and the toll is a gratuity.

infrastructure.victory: Unchanged: the Network condition still scores towns joined by road, rail and sea routes you built (victory.conditions network), and rail still scores victoryPointsPerTile as it is laid.
infrastructure.notes: None of this makes a road a private road. Anyone may walk it, and paying the toll is the price of the walk - which is exactly the relationship a turnpike had with the people who used it.

carrying.$comment:
What a figure carries on its own back, in kilograms, and the number that counts it down. It is BURDEN: the kilograms a figure can still take on. Its card prints the figure it starts with, the player board has a track for it, and a token walks DOWN it as things are picked up and back UP as they are put down. Strength has nothing to do with it any more - strength is for battle only (conflict.strength) - so a strong figure is not a strong porter unless its card says so.

Mass and bulk are two different measures and never mix: bulk is a commodity's storage-slot and shipping cost (commodities.json, transport.json), mass is what one item weighs (items.json massKg). Cargo in a cart is bulk; the axe on your shoulder is mass.
carrying.$scaleNote: Burden is a printed kilogram figure on every card, 0 to the board's ceiling of 20 (playerboard.json), and the figures on the cards that existed before burden had a track were each a strength times three, which is where a character's number started from. A figure with no card of its own - a worker, a soldier, a hireling - starts with the burden of its people (peoples.json burden.base).
carrying.limit: the Burden the card prints, in kilograms, which is what the figure has left to take. A figure with no card of its own uses its people's burden.base (peoples.json).
carrying.marker: The B track on the player board. Set it from the B box on the card at setup, knock it down by the mass of everything picked up and by the purse at perKg, and put it back up by what is put down or spent. It cannot go below 0: a figure may not take up what it has no kilograms left for.
carrying.limitRule: A figure may not take up an item, or a purse, that would take its Burden below 0. Load it onto a vehicle, hand it to someone with room, or leave it where it lies.

coin.$comment:
Coin was on the list below - weightless, an abstraction, the one thing a figure could hold an unlimited quantity of. It is not any more. A gold coin weighs 25 grams (currency.massKgEach), forty to the kilogram, and it goes on the scales with the sword and the rope.

What that buys is a real decision at the top of the game. A figure starting at 9 kg of burden is carrying a fortune at 360 coin; one starting at 18, twice that. Spend that on plate and a greatsword and there is nothing left for a fortune, and a party that has just sold a hold of jewellery has to work out how it is getting the money home. Coin is not a number in a corner of the sheet any more, it is cargo.
coin.counts: Against the same limit as everything else. Total what the figure is wearing, wielding, stowing and carrying in its purse.
coin.elsewhere: Coin in a strongbox on a wagon is cargo like any other and is measured in bulk, not on a figure's back. Coin left in a town is not being carried by anybody.

notCarried: Commodities in transit, which travel by transport mode and are measured in bulk.
Mana, in the body or in a talisman - the talisman itself has mass, its charge does not.
carrying.onZeroHealth: A figure carried to a settlement at 0 health loses everything it was carrying on the way.
carrying.notes: Burden has had three lives: a bar up the right edge of every card, then nothing at all while strength swallowed it, and now a track again. It came back because a limit that is only a sum at the table is a sum nobody does, and a token that walks down as the pack fills is one everybody can see.

upkeep.$comment:
What a figure spends by being alive, and which of its numbers it spends. FOOD and WATER are kept apart on purpose and cost different things: food is a meal every round, counted off a ration card on the road and off the town's stock at home, and going without it costs STRENGTH; water is a clock (Thirst) that only climbs where there is no water, and at the top of it a figure bleeds HEALTH. Hunger weakens; thirst kills. Sleep keeps strength up. None of the three stands in for another: a party can be fed and parched, watered and starving, or fed, watered and exhausted.

There used to be a Hunger clock beside Thirst, its twin on its own ladder. It went when every figure started eating every round the way a worker always has: a clock that a meal knocks four rungs off is a clock nobody ever watched, where a K ladder on a sack of bread going down a rung a day is a thing a player can see running out. The column it freed went to Wisdom.

What makes the two different in play is WHERE they are got. Water is free wherever there is water - a town, a river, a lake, a marsh - and nowhere else, so it is a question of the map. Food is never free away from your own town, so it is a question of the purse. The desert asks the first question hard (terrain.json desert upkeep.thirst); the cold asks the second (terrain.json upkeep.meals).

food.atHome: In a town of your own, your hero is one more mouth in the Feeding phase: counted with the workers and fed from the town's stock at population.foodPerWorkerPerRound. A worker and a hero eat alike.
food.onRoad: Anywhere else, the figure eats one meal a round off a provision card in its kit (items.json, class provision): knock that card's K ladder down a rung in the Feeding phase.
food.terrain: A round ended on a hex whose terrain prints upkeep.meals (terrain.json) costs that many meals more: cold is hungry work.

refill.where: At any inn or any market, buy meals back onto a provision card, up to its K box, at this price each. In your own town a unit of food from stock fills one meal instead.
refill.note: A town's own market sells meals at the same price whoever owns it, and the coin goes to the board.

missed.note: A round with no meal costs the figure 1 strength. Sleep does not give back strength lost to an empty belly until the figure has eaten again: a fed figure that sleeps gets all of it back as usual. Hunger weakens; it does not wound. Thirst does that.

thirst.terrain: A round ended on a hex whose terrain prints upkeep.thirst (terrain.json) raises Thirst by that much more. A desert is three rungs a round, not one.

eased.note: One draught drunk takes this many rungs off Thirst: from a waterskin (items.json waterskin) or a wineskin, or a cup at an inn. Thirst cannot go below 0.

thirst.freeWater: A figure that ends a round in a settlement, or on a river, lake or marsh hex, drinks for nothing: Thirst back to 0, and any waterskin it carries filled. Salt water is not drink - no sea hex waters anybody.

atLimit.note: At 20 the figure loses 1 health a round until it drinks, and drinking stops the losing without putting the health back (rest.medicalAid).

thirst.appliesTo: Every figure, on the road or in a town - but a town is a well, so in a town it never climbs.

night.camp: A party that stops before dark and makes camp restores every figure's strength to the number printed on its card. A bed at an inn does the same and costs rest.cost.
night.noCampNote: A party that travels a night leg, or ends the round without stopping, loses 1 strength from every figure in it. That is on top of the extra discovery roll a night leg already draws (movement.legs.nightRisk).
night.cumulative: Strength lost this way stacks night after night, and at 0 strength a figure does not fight (playerboard.json strength.atZero). Two hard nights turn a caravan guard into a passenger.

upkeep.notes: This is the pressure that makes a lantern, a granary, an inn and a stretch of salted meat worth their coin - and the reason a shorter leg with a camp at the end of it often beats a longer one without.

charisma.$comment: How well a figure is liked by things that could go either way. It is a rating, not a clock: only drink moves it in play, and only until the next sleep, and the card prints what it starts at. For now it does one job; it is expected to grow more, and each one gets a line here rather than a new rule in a chapter.

befriend.adds: Add the figure's Charisma to the d6 rolled to befriend a monster (monsters.json encounterOptions.befriend). The figure making the offer is the one whose Charisma counts.

charisma.scale: 0 to the board's ceiling. Characters run 1 to 6; monsters and vehicles print 0.
charisma.drink: Raised for a while by drink (drink.perDraught) - the one thing in play that moves it.
charisma.growth: Open. Haggling and hiring are the obvious next places for it to add; neither is a rule until a chapter adopts it. A toll talked down is Renown's job, not Charisma's.

test.$comment: One way to ask whether a figure manages something, used everywhere a card asks: roll a d6 and add one of the figure's numbers. Befriending is a test of Charisma against charisma.befriend.threshold; a task card names its own characteristic and its own number. A test is never a battle - nothing on the other side rolls.
test.rule: Roll the d6 and add the characteristic the card names. Equal to the card's number or over it passes.

wisdom.$comment: What a figure knows and notices: the number a task card tests more than any other, and the one drink takes away. It is a rating like Charisma - set from the card at setup and left alone - but it is a LASTING number: it rises only at a level milestone, and what it has risen to is written on the character record sheet and carried into the next game.
wisdom.tests: Task cards (data/tasks.json) test it more than anything else: d6 + Wisdom against the card's number (test).
wisdom.drink: Knocked down for a while by drink (drink.perDraught), and put back at the next sleep.
wisdom.scale: Characters print 1 to 6. Monsters and vehicles have no Wisdom box and no Wisdom marker.
wisdom.grows: Only at a level milestone (level.milestones), and never past the board's ceiling.

drink.$comment: Ale, wine and mead - everything in commodities.json category `drink` - make a figure better company and worse judgement. It is the cheapest way in the game to raise Charisma for a befriending roll or a hard bargain, and it is paid for in Wisdom, which is what a task card tests. Drunk, it also slakes thirst, so a wineskin is a waterskin that costs you something.
drink.what: A draught of anything in the drink category of commodities.json, from a wineskin (items.json wineskin) or by the cup at an inn.
drink.thirst: A draught of drink eases Thirst exactly as a draught of water does (upkeep.thirst.eased).
drink.lasts: Until the figure next sleeps, at a camp or in a bed. Then put its Charisma marker back to its card's box and its Wisdom marker back up by as many rungs as drink took off.
drink.floor: Wisdom cannot go below 0. A figure whose Wisdom reaches 0 by drinking is drunk: it does nothing else that round - no leg, no job, no task - fights only if something attacks it, and sleeps where it stands.
drink.cupNote: A cup at any inn. At an inn another player owns, the coin goes to them.

level.$comment:
How far a hero has come, 0 to 20, and the slowest number in the game on purpose. It rises on DEEDS - quests done and task cards done - and the deeds it wants grow with every level, so a hero gains several levels in a first game and one or two in a tenth. Reaching 20 is a career, not a game: tools/simulate.mjs plays careers out and fails if 20 ever comes inside one game, or never comes at all.

It is the one number that a hero takes home. The L marker shows it during a game; the character record sheet (data/recordsheet.json) keeps it, and the deeds counted toward the next one, between games.

deeds.quest: A mini quest done is worth its complexity in deeds (quests.json complexity). Each stage of a campaign quest done is worth the campaign's complexity.
deeds.task: A task card done is worth the deeds it prints (data/tasks.json deeds).
deeds.counted: On the character record sheet, in pencil, never on the board.

level.questGate: A quest card may print a minimum level (quests.json minLevel). A hero whose L marker is below it may read the card but not accept it: it goes to the bottom of the deck, as a declined card does, and costs nothing. The gate is on accepting only; a quest already held is never taken away by anything.
level.toNext: To rise to a level costs perLevel deeds for every step of the level being reached: 1 deed to reach level 1, 2 more to reach level 2, 3 more for level 3. Strike the deeds off when the level is taken; what is left over counts toward the next.
level.toTopNote: The sum of every step from 1 to the top, at perLevel a step. Stated so a chapter can print it; tools/validate-data.mjs recomputes it and fails if it is wrong.

milestones.note: On reaching a level that is a multiple of `every`, choose one rise and write it on the record sheet. It raises that number's box for this game and every game after. No rise may take a number past the board's ceiling; one that would is chosen again.

renown.$comment: What people say about a hero. Quests raise it and giving them up lowers it, and it pays in coin a player never has to count: every toll they are asked for is smaller and every hireling cheaper. It is the world's opinion, so most of it stays in the world when the game ends - a hero starts the next game with one renown for every level milestone they have passed, and earns the rest again.

gain.note: And whatever a task card prints.

loss.note: Giving up an accepted quest costs this. Renown cannot go below 0.

renown.stepsNote: Read the highest step the marker has reached. tollOff comes off every toll the figure's party is asked for - a road, a rail line, bandits, an event - and hireOff off every hireling's fee. Neither takes a price below 0.
renown.startsAt: At setup, one renown for every level milestone the hero has passed (level.milestones.every). Everything above that was this game's and is not carried.

career.$comment: A hero is not dealt fresh every game. At the end of one a player copies the numbers that last onto the CHARACTER RECORD SHEET (data/recordsheet.json, printed by tools/build-record.mjs) and brings the sheet to the next game. What lasts is what the hero IS - how far they have come and what they know. What they OWN does not: coin, kit, wounds and the contents of a pack belong to one game's economy and start fresh in the next, so a veteran is never a rich man walking into a poor table.
career.setUp: Set the board from the card as usual, then from the sheet: the L marker at the recorded level, every box a rise has raised raised by it, and Renown at renown.startsAt.
career.endOfGame: Write the level, the deeds left over, and any rise taken this game on the sheet's next row. Wisdom is written sober - as it stands after a night's sleep.
career.table: A table may agree to start everybody at level 0 for a game. A recorded hero is still the same hero afterwards: their sheet is simply not written on.

legs.day: Every moving figure, party or vehicle gets one day leg per round, at the speed in data/travel.json for its mode and the terrain letter codes it crosses.
legs.night: After its day leg a party may push on into the dark - but only with a lit torch or lantern, and slower. Night speeds, and what each light allows, are in data/travel.json.
legs.nightRisk: A party that travels a night leg makes a second discovery roll where it stops, with the monster band widened by 1. The dark is not neutral.

movement.notes: Figures (prospectors, merchants, soldiers, characters) use move points. Cargo uses transport modes with capacity and speed - see transport.json. The printed speed table by mode, terrain code and time of day is data/travel.json.

discovery.when: When a figure, party or vehicle ends its movement leg, roll once on the discovery table for the hex it stopped in - one roll for the leg, not one per hex crossed.
discovery.tables: data/discovery.json, one column per terrain letter code, with road and rail overrides
discovery.placement: Any result that persists - a monster, a trace, a cave, a quest site - is marked on the hex with a tile or figure so the whole table can see it.

encounter.$comment: What to DO with a discovery roll that turns up a living thing, which the tables have always produced and the rules have never said how to run. The answer is the one piece of furniture already on the table: a player board. The thing you met gets one, and for the length of the encounter it is a player - a player who is not a person.
encounter.rule: Shuffle the deck the result names - monsters for a beast, characters for a stranger on the road - and deal one card face up onto a spare player board, into the character recess.
encounter.setUp: Set that board's tracks from the card exactly as a player sets their own at setup: health, strength, pace and mana off the printed strip. Its armour is a number on the card and does not move, so nothing walks it. It now has everything a player has and is run the same way, by whoever is to the left of the player who drew it.
encounter.boards: Print one player board per player plus one for the table. The spare is the encounter board, and it is why the board is generic (playerboard.json board.generic): the furniture does not care whether a person or a wolf is sitting behind it.
encounter.afterwards: When the encounter ends the card is put away - back into its deck, or onto the hex as a lair, or into the winner's hand if it was befriended, enslaved or domesticated (monsters.json encounterOptions). Clear the board's tokens. Nothing about the encounter is written down.
encounter.why: A monster with a board is a monster whose health and strength are visible to everyone, walked down in front of the table rather than tracked in one player's head - and a stranger met on the road is set up exactly like a hero, because that is exactly what they are to themselves.

discovery.notes: Discovery is what you find when you are NOT looking. Prospecting, foraging and hunting have their own recipes and roll tables, and a discovery roll never replaces a survey.

exploration.notes: A prospector entering a face-down tile flips it. Flipping reveals terrain immediately; deposits need a survey roll on top of that.

rest.$comment: Two different kinds of hurt, mended two different ways. Strength is spent, so sleep gives it back. Health is damage, so only a healer does. That split is what makes a night's camp a decision rather than a formality, and it is what makes a physician worth feeding.
rest.where: Any settlement with an inn - every printed settlement has one; a player-built town needs the inn building. A camp made on open ground counts for strength and for nothing else.
rest.restoresStrength: All of it. One night's sleep sets the strength token back to the number printed on the card, wherever that night is taken - unless the figure went without a meal that round (upkeep.food.missed), when it gets nothing back until it has eaten.
rest.restoresHealth: None. Sleeping through a wound does not close it - see medicalAid.

medicalAid.$comment: The only thing that puts health back. Everything on this list is a person, a building or a bottle: health is repaired by somebody, never by time.
medicalAid.physicianNote: A character whose card says so - Doctor Elspeth Marrow, for one - mends this much anywhere they stand, with no infirmary and no town.
medicalAid.potion: items.json potion-healing, which mends on the spot and is drunk doing it.

cost.note: Per round of care. Waived in your own town, and at any inn or infirmary a quest reward names.
A bed for the night. Waived in your own town, and at any inn a quest reward names. A camp on open ground is free.

rest.notes: A resting character does nothing else that round. Vehicle damage is repaired separately - 1 box per round in any settlement of town rank or better, paying 5 coin per box.

hirelings.where: Hired at any inn, in any settlement of village rank or better.
hirelings.$statsNote: Every figure in a fight needs a strength and something to swing, hirelings included - conflict.battle totals both off whoever is fighting. These are the numbers printed on the inn's board, and they are what you are paying for: the thug is strong and carries nothing, the militiaman is ordinary and is wearing a coat of plates, and the blade is better than either and rolls a third die.

options.name: Thug
options.note: Refuses to fight monsters of strength 4 or more. Counts as a soldier for escort purposes.

options.name: Hired Blade
options.note: Fights anything, and rolls a third blue die, keeping the best two.

hirelings.notes: A hireling escorts one journey - a travelling party or a cargo in transit - then goes home. Hirelings eat no food; the fee is everything. An escorted cargo drops its theft risk to 0, same as a soldier escort. They do not eat and they do not sleep on your account either, so upkeep never touches them.

conflict.$comment:
A battle is ONE SUBTRACTION and it is the same subtraction the market makes.

It used to be a to-hit roll: one die per unit, hit on a 4, shifted by your strength and their defence, clamped at both ends, with armour cancelling hits after they landed. That is four numbers, two of them doing nearly the same job, and a table that had to remember which way the clamp went.

Now both sides total up and the difference is the wound. You roll TWO BLUE dice and add your strength and your gear; the thing you are fighting rolls TWO RED and adds its own. Whoever is lower loses health equal to the gap. Blue is what you want, red is what stands in your way, and it is the identical gesture a player has already made once this round on the market board - two blue against two red, subtract, read the difference. One pair of colours, two systems, no second thing to learn.

DEFENCE IS GONE. It was the half of the old strength that made a strong thing hard to hurt, and it was a good fix for a to-hit roll. In an opposed total there is nothing for it to do that armour was not already doing: a stone boar that barely swings and turns a sword is a low strength and a high armour, which is two numbers saying two things, where strength-and-defence was two numbers saying one.

battle.$comment: The one line of arithmetic printed on the player board, because it is the only one a player needs while a monster card is face up in front of them.
battle.rule: Both sides total strength, gear and dice. The lower total loses health equal to the difference.
battle.formula: yours = your strength + your gear + 2 blue dice · theirs = its strength + its armour + 2 red dice · the lower loses health = the difference
battle.gear: Your weapon's battle number plus every piece of armour you are wearing. A monster's gear is its armour and nothing else - its weapon is itself.
worked: Strength 4 with a sword (+1) and a leather jerkin (+1) rolls 7 on the blue: 13. A cinder wolf, strength 2, armour 1, rolls 7 on the red: 10. The wolf takes 3 - and it has 4 health, so one more exchange finishes it.
The same character against Vhalrik, strength 7, armour 3, who rolls 8: 18 against 13. The character takes 5, which is half of what they have.
Equal totals wound nobody. Two figures who are the same and roll the same have had a fight and neither of them has anything to show for it, which is the honest answer.
battle.ties: A difference of nothing is no damage to anybody.
battle.$simultaneousNote: There is only one roll and only one loser, so hits are no longer applied both ways. Attacking is still never free: the dice decide who was better on the day, and being the attacker buys nothing at all.
battle.extraDice: A few cards grant an extra die of your own colour - Ruk's escort trait, a hired blade. Roll it and KEEP THE BEST TWO. It is the only place in the game where more dice are rolled than are counted, and it is worth about a point and a half.
battle.appliesTo: Any figure with a strength: characters (characters.json), monsters (monsters.json), and hirelings, which fight at the numbers printed on the inn's board.

strength.$comment: One number, one job: strength is what you SWING WITH, the base of your side of the battle roll, and it is still the threat threshold some rules read off a monster card. It no longer carries anything - that is Burden (carrying) - so strength is for battle only. It is also the number a hard night takes off you (upkeep.night): an exhausted figure fights worse, and that is one token moving down one track.
strength.scale: 0 to the board's ceiling (components.json board.track). Characters run 2 to 6, monsters 2 to 7.
strength.carries: Nothing. Strength is for battle only; what a figure can carry is its Burden (rules.json carrying).
strength.inABattle: It is added to your total, straight, once. It never adds dice - everyone rolls two, and the very few things that grant a third say so on their own card.
strength.threshold: Unchanged and read off the same number: a thug refuses a monster of strength 4 or more, monsters of strength 4+ get a free round against a fleeing cargo vehicle, and a boar spear earns its +3 against anything of strength 4 or more that charges.
strength.atZero: A figure at 0 strength does not fight.

armour.$comment: What is between you and the blow, and the only piece of gear a monster has. It used to be two things - DEFENCE, which stopped a hit landing, and ARMOUR, which cancelled it after it had. In an opposed total there is no difference between those two sentences: both of them are a number that makes the other side's roll less likely to hurt you. So there is one number, it is called armour, and a monster's hide is on the same field as a suit of plate.
armour.scale: 0 upward. A worn suit runs 1 to 3, and a figure wearing body, head and off-hand can reach 5. Monsters run 0 to 3.
armour.adds: Straight to your battle total, once per piece worn.
armour.wears: One wear point per round of battle, on every piece worn - see rules.json wear. A blow you turned still dented the plate.
armour.$monsterNote: A monster's armour is what its card prints in the A box, and it is the whole of the old defence rescaled: an ash drake is strong AND armoured, a rime harpy is neither, and a stone boar barely swings and still turns a sword.

flee.$comment: The option a party has always had, and now the one it has to earn. Fleeing used to be free - withdraw the way you came, lose your discovery roll, done - which made every monster optional and most of them decorative. You have to be FASTER than the thing you are running from, and half the bestiary is faster than a person on foot.
flee.rule: A party may run only if its pace is GREATER than the monster's. Equal is not greater: a thing that matches you stays with you.
flee.pace: The party's pace for the leg it is on - the number on the P track, off travel.json for its mode and the ground. The monster's is printed on its card.
flee.succeeds: Withdraw the way you came and end your movement. No discovery roll this leg, and nothing is looted.
flee.refused: A party that cannot outpace the monster may not decline the fight. It may still befriend it, or offer it something, or die.
flee.cargo: Monsters of strength 4 or more get one free round of the battle roll against a fleeing cargo vehicle, whatever its pace.
flee.$whyNote: It puts a road, a horse and a night's sleep into the same decision as a sword. A mounted party outruns nearly everything; a party on foot at the end of a hard week has a pace of 2 and outruns a mire strangler and nothing else.

conflict.notes: One roll, one loser, one wound. Both sides total strength, gear and dice; the lower total loses health equal to the difference; and a tie hurts nobody.

conditions.name: Prosperity
conditions.summary: Points for fed population, completed buildings and luxury goods held at game end.

conditions.name: Industry
conditions.summary: Points for the depth of your longest completed production chain and for each tier-3 good produced.

conditions.name: Network
conditions.summary: Points for towns connected by road, rail and sea routes you built.

victory.notes: Scoring is deliberately plural so that a mining-and-rail strategy and a farming-and-trade strategy can both win.
